newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco talks resume after tobacco verdict.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco talks resume after tobacco verdict.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

State attorneys general resumed settlement talks with cigarette makers Monday afternoon with the aim of tackling the difficult issue of whether there can be a cap on the industry's liability without cutting off lawsuits.
Following an afternoon meeting with tobacco company executives, Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore told reporters he was optimistic about the progress being made.
"The industry continues to concede issues ... there is no talk of immunity" from lawsuits, Moore said.
The top state law officers broke into small groups to discuss the afternoon's developments and were to resume negotiations with tobacco officials Tuesday morning.
The negotiations began shortly after a Jacksonville, Fla., jury awarded a verdict in favor of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco in a case brought by the family of a smoker who died of lung cancer.
Attorneys general said the verdict would have no effect on the negotiations.

"This was an individual case. All the attorneys general that are here today in Dallas in order to talk to the industry, we are talking about our state cases," Florida Attorney General Robert Butterworth told reporters.

At least 25 state attorneys general have sued the industry to recoup Medicaid health care costs of smokers and to obtain other concessions from cigarette makers, including efforts to reduce youth smoking.
Butterworth was asked if the verdict would have an impact on talks with the tobacco firms.
"Not at all," he said. "I really do not believe this gives them any strength."

Arizona Attorney General Grant Woods said that each of the individual smokers' lawsuits are very fact-specific and "they are going to turn as much on the conduct of an individual smoker as they are on the conduct of the industry.
"That is not the case with these state lawsuits ... the conduct of the tobacco industry will be what's on trial, period," Woods said.
Thomas Griscom, executive vice president of external relations at R.J. Reynolds Tobacco, told reporters as he entered negotiations that he also did not think the verdict would affect talks.
"I don't think the court case has at all been tied in to the sessions here. That case has been out there for some time," he said.

Mississippi's Moore said a group of attorneys general -- along with representatives of the health community, including influential former American Medical Association President Lonnie Bristow -- would discuss public health and civil liability issues in Monday afternoon's session with tobacco representatives.
The attorneys general have said they would never agree to a settlement that would protect the tobacco industry from all litigation.

When asked by reporters whether the tobacco industry had given up on the idea of total immunity, Moore replied, "These guys don't give up on anything, but we're making progress on that issue," he said.
Richard Scruggs, a Mississippi lawyer who is assisting the state in its litigation, said the attorneys general had swapped ideas on the liability issue with industry officials in recent days.

The industry, which began negotiating directly with the attorneys general early last month, has been dealt several big blows recently. The most damaging was last month's ruling by a Greensboro, N.C., federal judge, who once represented tobacco growers as a private attorney, that held the Food and Drug Administration has the power to regulate tobacco.

Although the judge said the FDA did not have the authority to regulate advertising of cigarettes, the Supreme Court refused a few days later to hear a challenge to a Baltimore law restricting placement of tobacco billboards.

Legal experts predicted the move would strengthen efforts by cities and towns to restrict tobacco ads and just last week a proposal was made in New York City to ban tobacco billboards and promotions near schools and other locations where children gather. Washington State's King County, which encompasses Seattle, is expected to vote on a similar proposal on May 30.
